summary.text: Phylogenetics is the study of the evolutionary history of life, using observable characteristics of organisms or genes.
Its result is a phylogenetic tree, a diagram of the hypothetical relationships among organisms that reflects their inferred evolutionary history.
It is used in fields such as cancer research, drug discovery and forensic science, for example to screen for closely related species that may share a useful trait.

items.prompt: A diagram links species by relatedness but marks no starting point or shared ancestor at its base. What kind of diagram is it?

options.label: A Linnaean table
An unrooted tree
A rooted tree
A narrative scenario

items.explain: An unrooted tree does not show the origin or root of the taxa, while a rooted tree indicates their hypothetical common ancestor.

items.prompt: A researcher finds a fossil and wants to place it on a tree of life. Where does it go?

options.label: At a tip, where living taxa also sit
Only at the root, since fossils are old
Fossils can't go on trees, only living species
Along the branches, never at a tip

items.explain: The tips of a phylogenetic tree represent the observed entities, which can be living taxa or fossils.

items.prompt: Two patients carry HIV samples that are closely related. Can a lab prove from this that one infected the other?

options.label: Yes; close relatedness proves who infected whom
Yes; but only if the samples were taken in one year
No; HIV genes do not differ between people
No; it cannot be the sole proof and shows no direction

items.explain: Phylogenetic analysis can track differences in HIV genes, but it cannot be the sole proof of transmission and does not show its direction.

items.prompt: Chemists have found a useful venom in one fish. How can a phylogenetic tree help them look for more?

options.label: It shows which distant species evolved different venoms
It limits the search to fish, the only venomous group
It points to close relatives that may share the trait
It cannot help, so every species must be tested at random

items.explain: Scientists screen for closely related species that may have the same useful traits, and a tree shows which related fish may also carry the trait.

items.prompt: Two biologists in the 1940s each tell a different story of how some animal groups are related, with no scoring rule. Why is it hard to decide who is right?

options.label: Such stories were often ambiguous, with no explicit criteria
Such stories ignored every observable trait of the organisms
Such stories relied too heavily on modern DNA sequence data
Such stories were never allowed to include any fossil taxa

items.explain: Before 1950, inferences were generally narrative scenarios, which were often ambiguous and lacked explicit criteria for evaluating alternative hypotheses.

items.prompt: A lab can read a fixed total number of DNA positions. Which sampling plan tended to give more accurate trees in the study described?

options.label: Many species, with only a few positions read for each
Fewer species, with more positions read for each
Both plans gave exactly the same accuracy every time
Accuracy depended only on the number of species

items.explain: With the same total number of sites, sampling fewer taxa with more sites per taxon showed higher accuracy in most of the models tested.
